title: Processor Affinity
body:
A [[Thread]]'s preference for the CPU it last ran on. Only means anything on a
multiprocessor, where the scheduler has a choice of where to put you.

The reason is entirely [[Cache]]. While a thread runs, the CPU it is on fills its cache
with that thread's code and data. Migrate the thread to a different core and none of that
comes with it: the new core's cache knows nothing about it, so the thread runs at memory
speed until it has warmed the new cache up. All that work is thrown away, and the old
core's cache is now full of lines nobody wants.

Two strengths:

- **Soft affinity**: the scheduler *tries* to keep you on the same CPU but will migrate you
  to balance load. The default.
- **Hard affinity**: you pin the thread to a CPU (or a set of them) and the scheduler is
  not allowed to move it. Used for real-time work and for benchmarking.

The tension is load balancing. Perfect affinity means an idle core sits idle while another
core's [[Ready Queue]] backs up; perfect balancing means threads bounce between cores and
nobody's cache is ever warm. Real schedulers migrate only when the imbalance is large
enough to be worth the cold cache.

Same shape as the argument in [[Cache]] about locality, one level up: keep the work near
the data it already touched.
